bluf: Production AI apps need designed systems, not only generated code.

slides.title: AI makes prototypes easy; production still needs system design
slides.subtitle: Executive briefing from Ras Mic's system-design walkthrough
points: The talk argues that AI-generated apps fail when they skip architecture decisions.
The proposed operating lens is explicit trade-offs across scale, reliability, speed, and cost.
The Pluto case study shows a practical stack for an AI-agent product built on managed abstractions.

slides.title: Use four design questions before choosing the stack
slides.subtitle: The speaker frames engineering as trade-off management, not tool collection
cards: Can the system absorb more users or data by adding capacity?
How likely is each provider or service to fail under real usage?
Will the architecture keep the product fast enough?
Which choices protect runway, and which deliberately buy speed?

slides.title: Modern app platforms compress heavy infrastructure work
slides.subtitle: The video positions cloud and managed platforms as abstraction layers
layers: High control; expensive and hard to scale

slides.title: Pluto is presented as an enterprise-oriented AI-agent app
slides.subtitle: The product context drives the architecture choices
points: Multiple client surfaces: web, desktop, mobile, and admin experiences.
Agent execution requires durable backend state, inference, sandboxed workspaces, and browser access.
The target buyer is business teams, which raises auth, compliance, monitoring, and reliability requirements.

slides.title: The core architecture separates experience, control plane, and specialized services
slides.subtitle: The deck recreates the speaker's final architecture map as editable PowerPoint shapes

slides.title: The recommended repo model keeps agents and developers aligned
slides.subtitle: One codebase gives AI agents enough context to work across surfaces
points: Start with a monorepo so web, mobile, desktop, backend, and services share context.
Use familiar, documented tools because AI coding agents are more reliable with common ecosystems.
Segment services only where the domain has a clean boundary and independent failure modes.

slides.title: Convex is treated as the control plane for product state and workflows
slides.subtitle: The backend choice is tied to data, actions, jobs, and agent-readable code
points: The speaker prefers Convex because backend behavior is expressed as code.
Workflows, scheduled jobs, queues, and external integrations are positioned as first-class backend needs.
The product's main state should remain simple enough for agents to understand and modify.

slides.title: Specialized services carry riskier domains outside the main app path
slides.subtitle: Inference, payments, and messaging are separated because they have distinct responsibilities

slides.title: Payments architecture should match the pricing model
slides.subtitle: The talk distinguishes subscription billing from credit-based usage
points: Stripe is framed as sufficient for straightforward subscription billing.
Autumn is chosen for Pluto because credits, top-ups, and consumption accounting are central to the product.
The inference ledger becomes a control point for tracking wallet balance and model-provider consumption.

slides.title: Observability is a production requirement, not a cleanup task
slides.subtitle: Once AI-generated code reaches users, failures need traceability
points: The speaker recommends Sentry and PostHog for error logging, analytics, and failure visibility.
The practical requirement is to know what failed, when it failed, and which path produced the issue.
Monitoring becomes more important as the system spans client, backend, services, and sandbox providers.

slides.title: The explicit trade-off is spending more to protect product experience
slides.subtitle: The case study prioritizes reliability and speed over early cost optimization
points: Separate services and larger sandbox resources increase cost.
The rationale is to keep agents fast and the product resilient while the business model is still learning.
Cost optimization is acknowledged as future work, not ignored as a non-issue.

slides.title: A repeatable AI-build playbook falls out of the walkthrough
slides.subtitle: Translate the case study into operating principles for future builds
steps: Define product surfaces and state boundaries
Choose managed abstractions where they reduce undifferentiated work
Keep everything in a monorepo until a service boundary is justified
Instrument errors, analytics, and usage ledgers before launch
Let AI optimize within a designed system, not invent the system live

slides.title: Decision: ship AI apps on deliberate architecture, not vibes
slides.subtitle: Client-ready checklist
cards: Does each tool reduce complexity the team would otherwise own?
Can the system explain why each service exists?
Can failures be observed, traced, and repaired quickly?
Do costs match the current growth and learning stage?
